questions.knowledge_point: Reducing an Inhomogeneous ODE to First-Order System
questions.problem:
The second-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+{e}^{t}{y}^{′}+2ty={t}^{2}
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-{e}^{t}{y}^{′}-2ty+{t}^{2}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-{e}^{t}{x}_{2}-2t{x}_{1}+{t}^{2}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-2t{x}_{1}-{e}^{t}{x}_{2}+{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
f(t)=-2t{x}_{1}-{e}^{t}{x}_{2}+{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}-{t}^{2}{y}^{′}+6ty=-3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t)$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},$ ${x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}={t}^{2}{y}^{′}-6ty-3.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}={t}^{2}{x}_{2}-6t{x}_{1}-3.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-6t{x}_{1}+{t}^{2}{x}_{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
f(t)=-6t{x}_{1}+{t}^{2}{x}_{2}-3.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing an Inhomogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
questions.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+3y={e}^{2t}$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where

| $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,,\,f(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-3}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-4}} | {{field-5}} |  |  | {{field-6}} |  |  |  |

and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t)$ and ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-2{y}^{′}-3y+{e}^{2t}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}+{e}^{2t}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
The third-order differential equation ${y}^{‴}+2t\,{y}^{″}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{y}^{′}={e}^{t}$ can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ where

| $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,A=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | $1$ | {{field-1}} |  | $\,,\,f(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-3}} |  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |
|  | $0$ | $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ | {{field-5}} |  |  | {{field-6}} |  |  |  |

and for $y=y(t),$ we have $y={x}_{1}(t),$ ${y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t),$ and ${y}^{″}={x}_{3}(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-2t\,{y}^{″}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{y}^{′}+{e}^{t}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-2t\,{x}_{3}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{2}+{e}^{t}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{2}-2t\,{x}_{3}+{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -2t\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]
$$
